Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette:
Minh is a 74-year-old retired welder, married for over fifty years, who came to the clinic at his wife's urging after years of silent suffering. He was born in a small village in Vietnam and lived through the war as a civilian. One afternoon in 1968, during what he later learned was a bombing run by American planes, he was caught outside his home. The explosions threw him into a ditch, and he lay there for hours, choking on dust and smoke, unable to draw a full breath while the ground shuddered with each impact. He remembers fragments-the smell of burning thatch, the screaming of a neighbor's water buffalo-but much of that day remains a jumble of disconnected sensations. The memory feels alien to him, as if it happened to someone else, and the story itself seems too extreme to be real; he has sometimes wondered if he imagined it all.

After the war, Minh moved to the United States, became a welder, and raised a family. But the old sensations never fully left him. Certain car sounds-the rumble of a heavy engine or a backfire-would jerk him back to that ditch. When that happened, his memory would surge, not as a complete narrative but as visceral fragments: the pressure of the dirt, the terror of not being able to breathe. Because the memory returned so vividly, he began to see reminders everywhere-in the rumble of any engine, in a constricted chest, in the sight of an open field-as if the past had stained the present. He learned to redirect his thoughts quickly, forcing himself to think of something neutral-his workbench, the blue sky-to shut the intrusion down. He also began to avoid talking about the war altogether. What was the point? The people responsible had never faced any consequences, and he had come to believe that the event happened partly because he had not run fast enough or hidden better. That sense of injustice and self-blame made the memory even harder to discuss, so he stayed silent.

Over the decades, Minh found himself avoiding open spaces, especially fields or parking lots that felt exposed; he would walk along walls or stay close to buildings. The breathlessness-any feeling of being short of air, even from climbing stairs-would immediately trigger a flash of that afternoon, and he would become hypervigilant, scanning his surroundings for threats. He had difficulty concentrating at work because his mind was constantly on alert, and at night he struggled to fall asleep, needing to stay vigilant even in his own bedroom. The hypervigilance itself made him more sensitive to car sounds-every distant engine became a potential danger signal, which in turn triggered more intrusive memories.

Minh's wife noticed that he would sometimes stare at the television during war documentaries, then turn away without a word. Media coverage of conflicts anywhere in the world would resurrect that hollow feeling of his memory being incomplete, and he would retreat into redirection again. But avoiding these triggers only reinforced his sense that the event was too terrible to integrate, and the memory remained fragmented and alien. The self-blame deepened: if he had acted differently, perhaps he would have a complete memory, something that made sense. He had long felt that nothing had been done about the injustice, and that belief kept him on guard, ready for the next car sound, the next struggle for breath.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a panic attack in a supermarket parking lot when a truck backfired. He dropped to his knees, gasping, unable to speak, and his wife had to drive him home. That night, lying awake and alert, he realized he could no longer manage this on his own. He is afraid of what talking might do-that it will make the memory more real, or that he will be overcome by shame. But he also hopes, quietly, that perhaps there is a way to make the memory feel like his own, and to finally catch a full breath.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that the trauma memory directly causes triggers; instead, hypervigilance (threat) increases sensitivity to triggers, but the memory itself does not drive the occurrence or salience of triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the trauma memory directly causes triggers; instead, hypervigilance (threat) increases sensitivity to triggers, but the memory itself does not drive the occurrence or salience of triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
